title: RAG: retrieval metrics and Text-to-SQL vs RAG
seriesDescription: Chunking, embeddings, hybrid search, reranking and retrieval metrics. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Compute recall@k, precision@k, MRR and nDCG from small ranked lists, diagnose retrieval failures, and decide between RAG and Text-to-SQL.
source: Manning, Raghavan, Schutze: Introduction to Information Retrieval; Ragas docs; Liu et al., Lost in the Middle (2023); LangChain SQL docs; Pinecone learning centre

questions.prompt: Query 1 returns [d4, d1, d7, d2, d9] and its relevant set is {d1, d2, d5}. Query 2 returns [d3, d8, d5, d6, d1] and its relevant set is {d3}. Query 3 returns [d2, d4, d6, d8, d0] and its relevant set is {d9}. Compute the Mean Reciprocal Rank over the three queries, multiplied by 100.
questions.explanation: Reciprocal ranks: Query 1 first hit d1 at rank 2 gives 0.5; Query 2 hit at rank 1 gives 1; Query 3 never retrieves d9, so 0. MRR = (0.5 + 1 + 0)/3 = 0.5, i.e. 50.

questions.prompt: Query 1 returns [d4, d1, d7, d2, d9] and its relevant set is {d1, d2, d5}. What is precision@5 for this query, as a percentage?
questions.explanation: Two of the five returned documents (d1 and d2) are relevant, so precision@5 = 2/5 = 40%. Recall@5 for the same query would be 2/3, because d5 was never retrieved.

questions.prompt: A ranking has binary relevance [1, 0, 1] at positions 1, 2, 3 and the ideal ranking is [1, 1, 0]. With DCG = sum rel_i / log2(i + 1), compute nDCG@3 multiplied by 100, rounded to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: DCG = 1/log2(2) + 0 + 1/log2(4) = 1 + 0.5 = 1.5. IDCG = 1 + 1/log2(3) = 1.631. nDCG = 1.5/1.631 = 0.92. The log discount punishes pushing a relevant document down.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: MRR alone is a weak metric for questions whose answer needs several documents.
questions.reason: MRR uses only the rank of the first relevant result and ignores all others.

whys.a: Correct: after the first hit, MRR is blind to whether the other needed documents were retrieved, so recall@k or nDCG is needed too.
whys.b: R is not just a side fact; it is exactly why MRR is weak here.
whys.c: R is true by definition of MRR.
whys.d: A is true for multi-hop or multi-document questions.

questions.explanation: Pair MRR (how early is the first good hit) with recall@k (did we get everything we needed).

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Increasing k can lower recall@k for a fixed query.
questions.reason: Recall@k is the number of relevant documents in the top k divided by the total number of relevant documents.

whys.a: A is false, so it cannot be explained by anything.
whys.b: A is false, so the pair is not both-true.
whys.c: R is true, so this option is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because a larger k can only add documents, so the numerator cannot shrink while the denominator is fixed. R is a true definition.

questions.explanation: Recall@k is non-decreasing in k. Precision@k is the one that usually falls as k grows.

questions.prompt: Recall@20 of your retriever is only 55% on the golden set. Which changes are plausible fixes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Add BM25 hybrid search to catch exact terms and identifiers.
options.why: Right: lexical matching recovers items that embeddings blur.

options.text: Use structure-aware chunking so answers are not split across chunk boundaries.
options.why: Right: bad boundaries are a frequent cause of missed answers.

options.text: Switch to a more capable generation model.
options.why: The generator cannot use documents that were never retrieved.
Temperature affects generation, not what the retriever returns.

questions.explanation: Low recall points at the retriever or index: chunking, embeddings, hybrid, query rewriting, metadata filters. Fix generation only after recall is healthy.

questions.prompt: Match each retrieval symptom to the most targeted fix.

left.text: Queries with exact SKUs and error codes miss
The right chunk is found but sits at rank 15
A follow-up like "what about its price?" retrieves junk
Users ask for "invoices from Acme in 2024" and results mix all customers
Pricing tables are cut in half across chunks

right.text: Rewrite the query using chat history
Metadata filters on customer and date

questions.explanation: Name the symptom, then pick the stage to fix: query, index, retrieval, ranking, or generation.

questions.prompt: True or false: if recall@k is 100%, the RAG system is guaranteed to answer correctly.

options.why: Retrieval recall only says the evidence was retrieved.
Correct: the generator can still ignore, misread or bury the evidence (for example mid-context), so answer faithfulness must be measured separately.

questions.explanation: Evaluate retrieval and generation separately: recall@k and nDCG for retrieval, faithfulness and answer relevance for generation.

questions.text: {1} is the fraction of the relevant documents found in the top k, {2} averages the reciprocal rank of the first relevant hit, and {3} rewards relevant documents placed higher using a logarithmic discount.
questions.explanation: Use them together: recall@k for coverage, MRR for first-hit speed, nDCG for graded ordering quality.

questions.prompt: A user asks: "What was the total value of orders placed by EU customers last quarter?" Which design fits best?

options.text: Text-to-SQL against a read-only replica with a validated, SELECT-only query.
options.why: Right: exact aggregation over structured rows is what SQL is for.

options.text: Embed every order row and let the LLM add up the top 20 hits itself, for any date range.
options.why: A sample of rows cannot give a complete exact sum; the LLM would also be doing arithmetic.

options.text: Fine-tune the LLM on last year's order table so it remembers every order total already.
options.why: Fine-tuning is stale on arrival and cannot be exact or auditable.

options.text: Retrieve the policy PDFs about order handling, then ask the LLM to estimate the revenue.
options.why: Policy documents do not contain the transactional numbers.

questions.explanation: Rule of thumb: structured, exact, aggregate or join questions go to SQL; unstructured, fuzzy, document-grounded questions go to RAG; many assistants route between both.

questions.prompt: Which requests are better served by RAG over documents than by Text-to-SQL? Select all that apply.

options.text: What does our refund policy say about digital goods?
options.why: Right: the answer lives in prose and must be quoted from a source.

options.text: Summarise the termination clauses in this contract.
options.why: Right: unstructured text that needs grounded summarisation.

options.text: Sum revenue by region for the last 90 days.
options.why: Aggregation over rows is a SQL job, not a document-retrieval one.

options.text: List customers who ordered both product A and product B.
options.why: A join or intersection over structured data fits SQL.

questions.explanation: A senior answer mentions routing, access control per source, and showing citations or the executed SQL for auditability.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: Including the table schema with column descriptions in a Text-to-SQL prompt improves query accuracy.
questions.reason: Every extra table in the prompt consumes tokens, so very large schemas raise cost and latency.

whys.a: R is true but it is a cost fact; it does not explain why accuracy improves.
whys.b: Correct: schema context reduces hallucinated tables and columns (A true). The token-cost point (R) is also true but does not explain A; it is why big schemas need schema retrieval or pruning.
whys.c: R is true, so A-true-R-false is wrong.
whys.d: A is true; grounding on the real schema is standard practice.

questions.explanation: For large warehouses retrieve only the relevant tables and example queries, then generate SQL.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the correct option.
questions.assertion: A hybrid assistant can route each question to either a SQL tool or a document retriever.
questions.reason: A router that classifies questions is always correct, so routing needs no evaluation.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.b: R is false, not just unrelated.
whys.c: Correct: A is true (agentic routing is common), but routing errors are real and should be covered by the golden dataset.
whys.d: A is true, so this option is wrong.

questions.explanation: Add routing accuracy as its own metric, and include ambiguous questions in the eval set.

questions.prompt: Tables results(query_id, doc_id, rank) hold the retrieved lists and gold(query_id, doc_id) holds the relevant documents. Write one SQL query that returns the Mean Reciprocal Rank over all queries in gold, counting a query with no relevant hit as 0.

checks.label: finds the best rank per query

questions.model:
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(1.0 / h.first_rank, 0)) AS mrr
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT query_id FROM gold) q
LEFT JOIN (SELECT r.query_id, MIN(r.rank) AS first_rank
           FROM results r
           JOIN gold g ON g.query_id = r.query_id AND g.doc_id = r.doc_id
           GROUP BY r.query_id) h ON h.query_id = q.query_id;
questions.explanation: The inner query finds the rank of the first relevant hit per query; the LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE turns a miss into 0 so it still counts in the average (otherwise MRR is inflated). Other shapes pass, for example a window function. On the three-query example from the integer question this returns 0.5.
